points.title: The five concepts of economics and business
points.brief: The subject is built on five ideas, resource allocation and decision-making, the business environment, entrepreneurship, work and work futures, and consumer and financial literacy.

points.title: Asking an inquiry question
points.brief: A good inquiry question about an economic or business issue is open, focused on one issue, and can be answered with evidence.

points.title: Finding and organising information
points.brief: Information can come from government statistics, news, businesses and surveys. Note who made each source and when, and sort what you find under headings.

points.title: Cause and effect in economics
points.brief: A cause-and-effect relationship explains how one change leads to another, such as a drought cutting the supply of fruit and raising its price.

points.title: Costs and benefits of a decision
points.brief: Before deciding, list what each choice gives (benefits) and what it takes (costs), including money, time and effects on others.

points.title: Needs and wants
points.brief: Needs are things people must have to survive, such as food, water and shelter. Wants are things people would like but can live without.

points.title: Scarcity
points.brief: Resources such as land, labour, money and time are limited, but people's wants are unlimited, so not every want can be met.

points.title: The three economic questions
points.brief: Because of scarcity, every economy must decide what to produce, how to produce it and for whom to produce it.

points.title: Opportunity cost
points.brief: Opportunity cost is the next best choice given up when making a decision, such as the swim you miss by spending the afternoon riding your bike.

points.title: Using resources sustainably
points.brief: Using resources sustainably means meeting needs and wants today without leaving too little for people in the future.

points.title: First Nations exchange networks
points.brief: First Nations communities traded goods such as ochre, stone tools and food along trade routes, and shared resources through kinship ties, using limited resources carefully.

points.title: What a business is
points.brief: A business makes and sells goods or services. Businesses exist to meet people's needs and wants, to make a profit and to give people jobs.

points.title: Goods and services
points.brief: Goods are things you can touch, such as shoes. Services are things done for you, such as a haircut.

points.title: Ways businesses reach customers
points.brief: Businesses sell through shopping centres, markets, small local stores, remote community stores and online.

points.title: A business owned by First Nations Australians
points.brief: Many First Nations Australians run businesses, in areas such as tourism, art, food and construction, often to create jobs and support their communities.

points.title: Sole traders
points.brief: A sole trader is one person who owns and runs a business, keeps all the profit and is personally responsible for all its debts.

points.title: Partnerships
points.brief: A partnership is owned by two or more people who share the work, profits and debts, such as a firm of lawyers.

points.title: Companies
points.brief: A company, or corporation, is owned by shareholders. It is legally separate from its owners, so they can lose only what they put in.

points.title: Franchises
points.brief: In a franchise, a business owner pays to use another company's name, products and way of operating, such as a fast food chain.

points.title: Cooperatives and not-for-profits
points.brief: A cooperative is owned by its members, who share its benefits. A not-for-profit puts any surplus back into its purpose, such as a charity.

points.title: What an entrepreneur is
points.brief: An entrepreneur spots an opportunity, takes a risk and organises resources to start or grow a business.

points.title: Qualities of entrepreneurs
points.brief: Entrepreneurs tend to show initiative, creativity, willingness to take risks, persistence and the ability to lead others toward a shared vision.

points.title: Values in business decisions
points.brief: Entrepreneurs' values shape their choices, such as being honest with customers, treating workers fairly and following the law.

points.title: First Nations entrepreneurs
points.brief: First Nations entrepreneurs include community-run companies such as the Gumatj Aboriginal Corporation in north-east Arnhem Land, which runs businesses on its own Country.

points.title: What makes a business succeed
points.brief: Successful businesses usually meet a real need, plan well, manage money carefully, keep customers happy and adapt when things change.

points.title: Why people work
points.brief: People work to earn income, and also for purpose, skills, friendships and a sense of contributing to their community.

points.title: Types of work
points.brief: Work can be full-time, part-time or casual, paid or unpaid, such as volunteering or caring for family at home.

points.title: Ways to earn an income
points.brief: People earn income from wages and salaries, profits from a business, dividends from shares, rent from property, and government payments.

points.title: Work and identity
points.brief: Work can shape how people see themselves and their role in the community, and affects their standard of living.

points.title: Rights and responsibilities
points.brief: A right is something you are entitled to. A responsibility is something you are expected to do. Consumers and businesses have both.

points.title: Consumer guarantees
points.brief: Under Australian Consumer Law, products must be safe, work as described and last a reasonable time, or you can ask for a repair, replacement or refund.

points.title: Cooling-off periods
points.brief: Some contracts, such as those signed with a door-to-door seller, give a few days in which the buyer can change their mind and cancel.

points.title: Business responsibilities to consumers
points.brief: Businesses must meet safety standards, give honest information and recall products found to be unsafe.

points.title: Budgeting before you buy
points.brief: A budget compares money coming in with money going out, which helps you plan to save for something before you buy it.
